## On exactitude in science

> ...In that Empire, the Art of Cartography attained such Perfection that the map of a single Province occupied the entirety of a City, and the map of the Empire, the entirety of a Province. In time, those Unconscionable Maps no longer satisfied, and the Cartographers Guilds struck a Map of the Empire whose size was that of the Empire, and which coincided point for point with it. The following Generations, who were not so fond of the Study of Cartography as their Forebears had been, saw that that vast Map was Useless, and not without some Pitilessness was it, that they delivered it up to the Inclemencies of Sun and Winters. In the Deserts of the West, still today, there are Tattered Ruins of that Map, inhabited by Animals and Beggars; in all the Land there is no other Relic of the Disciplines of Geography.

## SD

Average doesn't tell us everything!

```{r}
library(tidyverse)

dat <- tibble(score_1 = rnorm(20000) + 4, 
       score_2 = rnorm(20000)/5 + 4) |>
      pivot_longer(everything())

dat |>
  group_by(name) |>
  summarise(mean = mean(value), 
            n = n())

dat |>
  ggplot() +
  geom_density(aes(x = value, fill = name)) +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(legend.position = "none")

```

Something something measure of spread

```{r}
dat |>
  group_by(name) |>
  summarise(mean = mean(value), 
            n = n(),
            sd = round(sd(value), 2))
```

If you've got data that's normal, the middle 95% of your data points will be within +- 2 standard deviations of the mean. That's wildly useful, for all sorts of things. A neat healthcare example: most blood tests in completely fit and well people vary. If you collect that data, and plot it, and you're lucky, it'll fall into a normal distribution (not always though). Here's some imaginary data for a biomarker I'm calling HLDSP1 (happy, lucky, data skills participant) which I've measured in 1000 made-up people. That plots out as follows:

```{r}
hldsp1 <- tibble(hldsp1 = rnorm(20000, 20, 5))

hldsp1 |>
  ggplot() +
  geom_histogram(aes(x = hldsp1))

hldsp1_mean <- mean(hldsp1$hldsp1)
hldsp1_sd <- sd(hldsp1$hldsp1)
```
That data has a mean of `r round(hldsp1_mean, 2)`standard deviation of `r round(hldsp1_sd, 2)`. That means that we'll find 95% of our values within a bit under twice the SD either side of the mean. On the graph:

```{r}
hldsp1_class <- hldsp1 |>
  mutate(class = case_when(hldsp1 > 1.96*hldsp1_sd + hldsp1_mean ~ "bigger",
                           hldsp1 <= hldsp1_mean - (1.96*hldsp1_sd) ~ "smaller",
                           TRUE ~ "within")) 

hldsp1_class |>
  ggplot() +
  geom_histogram(aes(x = hldsp1, fill = class))

hldsp1_class |>
  group_by(class) |>
  summarise(n = n()) |>
  mutate(sumn=sum(n)) |>
  rowwise() |>
  mutate(percent = 100 * n/sumn) |>
  select(-sumn)


  
```


are calibrated in this kind of way such that the middle 95%

Anscombe's quartet: have a quick butchers at your data in a simple graph before doing anything

## Why think about storytelling?

* this is a session about some aspects of telling stories with data
* it's needed because:
  * bad graphs are everywhere
  * and everyone has an opinion about what makes good graphs
  
## Bad graphs are everywhere

+ [Yes](https://i.insider.com/51cb1bda6bb3f7d47800003b?width=700&format=jpeg&auto=webp)
+ [Ugly charts](https://flowingdata.com/category/visualization/ugly-visualization/)
+ [badvisualisations](https://www.tumblr.com/badvisualisations)

## Everyone has an opinion about how to improve graphs

+ OCS [spreadsheet checklist](https://analysisfunction.civilservice.gov.uk/policy-store/further-resources-for-releasing-statistics-in-spreadsheets/) // [chart checklist](https://analysisfunction.civilservice.gov.uk/policy-store/charts-a-checklist/)
+ [Cole Nussbaumer Knaflic](https://www.storytellingwithdata.com/)
+ [Mike Mahoney](https://www.mm218.dev/blog.html#category=Tutorials)
+ [Hadley Wickham](http://stat405.had.co.nz/lectures/20-effective-vis.pdf)
+ [Jeffrey Hee](https://courses.cs.washington.edu/courses/cse442/17au/lectures/CSE442-VisualEncoding.pdf)

::: {.notes}
+ if you're a data viz person, or want to be one, you should read all of those (and more). You'll need all the details.
+ the rest of us can go a very long way with four simple storytelling principles
+ this session will look at these rules as applied to graphs. You could apply them to other areas of your work
:::

## The analyst's pitfall

+ Doing a piece of analysis gives you an odd perspective on an issue:
  + time served
  + starting expertise
  + power of details

::: {.notes}
+ Two cases:
  + How long did your last project take to create?
  + How long did you spend reading the last project report/dashboard/statistical output that you read?
  
+ you understand and know the bones of the project. You're driven by details.
+ your reader doesn't. The details are a barrier.

+ beware the comforting fallacy of including all the information for the sake of precision: it's a category mistake

+ you need to know it all, too: the domain knowledge is important
:::





## Four principles

+ Be obvious, and know what you want to say
+ Be explicit, and make that point directly to your audience
+ Be simple, and select the telling details
+ Be concise, and omit everything else


## Be obvious 

Know what you want to say

## Be obvious 

* most data sets can support lots of different conclusions
* it's your job to decide which conclusion a reader should draw
  * your knowledge of the data is key
  * lots of planning/storyboarding
  * lots of trying to boil down complicated data into simple stories

## Be explicit
Know your audience, and speak directly to them

* different groups will have different needs
  * communicating with other KIND people will present different demands to talking to managers
